extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and politicians concerned with the French Revolution (late-18th-century readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective political essay arguing for preservation of ancient manners, religion, and mixed institutions and warning about the moral and political consequences of the French Revolution. It evaluates the character of states and the causes of civil stability or decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of manners as national good
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be a system of manners in every nation which a well-informed mind would be disposed to relish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that to make us love our country, our country ought to be lovely; manners and opinions form an essential part of national health, and their destruction leaves society without a compass to govern it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power must stand on its own honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Power, of some kind or other, will survive the shock in which manners and opinions perish; and it will find other and worse means for its support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When usurpation destroys ancient principles it 'will hold power by arts similar to those by which it has acquired it,' leading to preventive murder, confiscation, and a political code of grim maxims rather than rule by honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ancient principles to avoid tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: When ancient opinions and rules of life are taken away, the loss cannot possibly be estimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their removal deprives society of a guiding compass; the author presumes ancient manners contributed beneficially to Europe's prosperity and warns that experimental destruction risks gross, ferocious, and sordid barbarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning depends on nobility and clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: The nobility and the clergy, the one by profession, the other by patronage, kept learning in existence, even in the midst of arms and confusions...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learning 'paid back' its protectors by enlarging their minds; if learning aspires to be master rather than instructor it will be 'debauched by ambition' and cast into the mire without its natural protectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and manufacture require moral foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even commerce and trade and manufacture... are themselves perhaps but creatures, are themselves but effects which, as first causes, we choose to worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trades grew under the same social shade as learning; losing the spirit of nobility and religion may cause commerce and the arts to decay, so economic prosperity depends on moral and institutional supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject vulgarity and coarse political proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Already there appears a poverty of conception, a coarseness, and a vulgarity in all the proceedings of the Assembly and of all their instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer criticizes revolutionary rhetoric and behavior: 'Their liberty is not liberal. Their science is presumptuous ignorance. Their humanity is savage and brutal.' Such qualities indicate moral and political decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as a moral school compared to real triumph
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre is a better school of moral sentiments than churches, where the feelings of humanity are thus outraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the stage, audiences would reject maxims that justify perfidy and murder for public benefit; tolerating such political computations in real life corrupts moral intuition and invites greater crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means cannot be justified by alleged public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifying perfidy and murder for public benefit, public benefit would soon become the pretext, and perfidy and murder the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing criminal means on the grounds of public advantage teaches preference for shorter criminal routes to ends, leading to rapacity, malice, and general moral decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between judgment and trust in rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: To degrade and insult a man as the worst of criminals and afterwards to trust him in your highest concerns... is not consistent to reasoning, nor prudent in policy, nor safe in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a leader is publicly denounced as criminal, then entrusting him with power is inconsistent and imprudent; punishment and civic trust must align with reason and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: National character rooted in inherited sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: We still bear the stamp of our forefathers... We have not (as I conceive) lost the generosity and dignity of thinking of the fourteenth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pamphlet values national continuity: habitual respect for tradition, religion, and institutions preserves dignity and guards against rapid social degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of useful prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice renders a man's virtue his habit, and not a series of unconnected acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than discarding all old prejudices, one should recognize that some embed practical wisdom, provide ready motives in emergencies, and convert duty into habitual virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward reformist arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: They have no respect for the wisdom of others, but they pay it off by a very full measure of confidence in their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes intellectuals who destroy old systems solely because they are old and who treat constitutions as mutable fashions rather than durable institutions worthy of attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mixed institutions in measured degree
rubrics_metrics.description: We cleave closely to them. We are resolved to keep an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced, mixed constitution—retaining elements of church, monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy in proper measure—provides stability; altering these degrees recklessly endangers continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: WE KNOW, AND WHAT IS BETTER, we feel inwardly, that religion is the basis of civil society and the source of all good and of all comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay holds that a religious establishment consecrates the state, instills awe and accountability in rulers and citizens, and supplies moral restraints that prevent societal collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of state offices to moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons possessing any portion of power ought to be strongly and awfully impressed with an idea that they act in trust, and that they are to account for their conduct in that trust to the one great Master...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who hold authority should feel their roles as quasi-religious trusts, looking beyond transient rewards to permanent moral responsibility; this helps prevent abuse of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on absolute popular authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect democracy is, therefore, the most shameless thing in the world. As it is the most shameless, it is also the most fearless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When popular authority is absolute, personal accountability and fear of infamy diminish; the people must be persuaded they are not the sole standard of right and wrong to avoid tyranny by the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment to office as selection for virtue and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: They will confer that power... on those only in whom they may discern that predominant proportion of active virtue and wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public office should be conferred not for petty interests or caprice but on individuals with proven virtue and wisdom suited to the charge; treating office as a 'holy function' preserves good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve jurisprudence and legal continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of jurisprudence... which with all its defects... is the collected reason of ages... would be no longer studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent, capricious changes to law undermine study and respect for jurisprudence; legal continuity links generations and maintains predictable grounds of hope and fear necessary for social order.
